title: ADHD pt 1
summary: Part one of a two-part Stuff You Should Know episode on ADHD (attention deficit hyperactivity disorder). Hosts trace the history of the diagnosis from an 1789 Scottish physician's description, through George Frederick Still's 1902 "defect of moral control," 1930s amphetamine experiments by Charles Bradley, Ritalin's development, and DSM revisions up to the 1994 three-type division. They then cover brain differences, genetics, dopamine and norepinephrine, executive function (working memory, inhibition, planning, time management, task shifting, decision making), default mode network, rejection sensitive dysphoria, hyperfocus and ADHD strengths. Part two is promised for a later episode.

entities.name: Rhode Island facility for children with neurological problems

segments.title: Content warning and cold open
segments.summary: Josh warns that the two-part ADHD episode discusses ADHD frankly and suggests parents of kids with ADHD preview it first.

segments.title: Opening banter and what ADHD is
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the two-part episode and explain ADHD as attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, noting its expanded understanding across kids, girls, and adults and the confusion over how the disorder is classified.

segments.title: Early descriptions of ADHD
segments.summary: Hosts say ADHD symptoms were described as early as 1789 by Scottish physician Sir Alexander Crichton, and that the condition is not simply a product of modern screens or sugar.

segments.title: Early 1900s to 1930s discoveries
segments.summary: George Frederick Still in 1902 described children with a defect of moral control, linked to impulsivity. In the 1930s, Franz Kramer and Hans Pollnow described hyperactivity, and in 1937 Charles Bradley at a Rhode Island facility found that Benzedrine made about half of the children treated less restless and more focused.

segments.title: Ritalin and psychiatric shifts
segments.summary: Hosts describe a gap before drug treatment became common, the 1950s shift toward prescribing, and Ciba Geigy developing Ritalin, named after the wife of chemist Leandro Panizzon. They then note early 20th-century views that developmental issues were brain injuries and the 1960s move away from that idea.
topics: brain injury theory of developmental disorders

segments.title: DSM-II and diagnostic naming
segments.summary: The DSM-II in the late 1960s introduced hyperkinetic reaction of childhood. Within about fifteen years it became attention deficit disorder (ADD), with subtypes based on hyperactivity.

segments.title: Genetics, adult diagnosis, and DSM-IV types
segments.summary: Hosts describe the 1987 naming of undifferentiated ADD, the 1990s discovery of a genetic component and adults being diagnosed, reasons ADHD was thought to be outgrown, and the 1994 DSM division into inattentive, hyperactive-impulsive, and combined types.

segments.title: Ad break
segments.summary: Sponsor break.

segments.title: Hosts' own ADHD diagnoses
segments.summary: Josh reveals he and Jerry both have ADHD and were diagnosed about a week apart. Chuck is the only one of the three without it. Hosts discuss how ADHD affects families and partners.

segments.title: ADHD brain differences and genetics
segments.summary: Josh says brain scans show structural differences in people with ADHD, such as smaller or differently sized regions, and that brain size does not indicate intelligence. He explains that impulses slip through because of difficulty regulating emotion and behavior. Chuck and Jerry note differences detectable as early as age four.

segments.title: Dopamine, norepinephrine, and motivation
segments.summary: Hosts explain that ADHD involves differences in dopamine and norepinephrine, with reduced reward feedback making routine tasks like cleaning less rewarding. Josh notes the current understanding is more dopamine transporters rather than less dopamine production. Fatigue and anxiety can compound this.

segments.title: Executive function overview
segments.summary: Josh and Jerry define executive function as the frontal lobe-based skills for prioritizing, handling distractions, and controlling impulses, and introduce six components that ADHD can impair, which vary in severity by person.

segments.title: Working memory, inhibition, and planning
segments.summary: Hosts explain working memory, self-restraint and inhibitory control including saying inappropriate things, and planning and problem solving, where people with ADHD may freeze when facing big tasks.

segments.title: Decision making, ADHD paralysis, and time management
segments.summary: Hosts describe decision making difficulties and ADHD paralysis, and say parents and partners can help break tasks into steps. Time management and the value of deadlines for people with ADHD are discussed.

segments.title: Forgotten deadlines and story of a missed meeting
segments.summary: Josh tells the story of an adult with ADHD who forgot to run a Monday meeting, which likely cost him a promotion. Hosts note forgetting deadlines is a common reason.

segments.title: Task shifting, everyday memory lapses, and back to one
segments.summary: Hosts describe set shifting and rigid thinking, a list of everyday ADHD struggles including forgotten bills and false memories, and walking into rooms and forgetting why. Josh and Chuck discuss the film term 'back to one' as a tip for recovering the thought.

segments.title: Default mode network
segments.summary: Hosts explain the default mode network as the brain regions active during daydreaming and idleness, and how in ADHD it may stay active during focused tasks. Josh cites Ned Hallowell describing a persistent pull toward distraction. Breathing and mindfulness are suggested.

segments.title: Ad break
segments.summary: Sponsor break.

segments.title: Rejection sensitive dysphoria
segments.summary: Hosts describe rejection sensitive dysphoria (RSD) as an intense emotional response to perceived rejection or criticism, which can be internalized or externalized and can make relationships hard. Some people with RSD become people pleasers. Studies suggest nearly all people with ADHD also have RSD, though it is not yet in the DSM.

segments.title: Hyperfocus and ADHD strengths
segments.summary: Hosts discuss hyperfocus as a possible superpower, a corporate study claiming neurodiverse workers produce 90 to 140 percent more work in engaging roles, and examples like detailing a car for an hour and a half. They also cover the view that neurodiverse people can succeed in any field if interested, dot-connecting, high energy, strong moral compass, infectious excitement, and catastrophic thinking as an asset.

segments.title: Wrap-up and sign-off
segments.summary: Josh says part one ends here and part two will continue the topic. The hosts note there is no listener mail for two-part episodes and sign off with the show's production credit.
